    AI Overview
    View all
    Lung cancer, the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, originates in the lungs, often from the air passages, with smoking being the primary cause, responsible for 80-90% of cases. Symptoms include a persistent cough, blood in sputum, chest pain, and weight loss. Diagnosis involves imaging (CT, PET, MRI) and biopsies, with treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, and targeted therapies determined by the subtype—non-small cell (NSCLC) or small cell (SCLC)
    . 
    Types of Lung Cancer 
    • Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC): The most common type (about 85% of cases). It includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma.
    • Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC): Less common but highly aggressive and tends to spread faster than NSCLC. 
    How Lung Cancer is Diagnosed 
    • Imaging Tests: CT scans, MRI scans, and PET scans are used to identify abnormal masses in the lungs.
    • Biopsy: A sample of tissue is removed and examined under a microscope to confirm cancer cells.
    • Sputum Cytology: Looking at sputum under a microscope to check for cancer cells.
    • Bronchoscopy: Using a camera on a thin tube to look inside the airways. 
    How Lung Cancer is Treated 
    • Surgery: Performed to remove the tumor and surrounding lung tissue, most common in early-stage cancers.
    • Chemotherapy: Uses drugs to kill cancer cells, often used for advanced disease or in combination with other treatments.
    • Targeted Therapies: Drugs that target specific molecular features of the cancer cells, particularly effective in non-smokers or specific genetic mutations.
    • Radiation Therapy: High-energy rays used to kill cancer cells, often used to shrink tumors or treat symptoms.
    • Immunotherapy: Helps the patient's own immune system fight the cancer. 
    Risk Factors and Prevention 
    • Smoking: The primary risk factor, but nonsmokers can also develop it.
    • Secondhand Smoke: Exposure significantly increases risk.
    • Radon Gas & Asbestos: Exposure to these substances is a major cause, especially in occupational settings.
    • Prevention: The most effective prevention is avoiding tobacco smoking and limiting exposure to environmental carcinogens. 
    Key Statistics & Trends 
    • Mortality: It is the leading cause of cancer death in both men and women.
    • Survival: Prognosis is highly dependent on early detection and the specific stage of the cancer.
    • Trends: While overall cases are decreasing due to lower smoking rates, there is a concerning rise in cases among younger, never-smoking individuals.
